I am 65 years old and have farmed these 8 mu in Quzhou County for 45 years. I know every inch of this land, and I have watched the wheat–maize system evolve from traditional practices to modern ones. With only two people in my household and some off-farm work to juggle, I cannot afford to waste labor or time, but my high school education and decades of experience have taught me that cutting corners on inputs costs more in lost yield than it saves in money.

This year, I will plant all 8 mu to winter wheat this autumn. I will use an improved semi-dwarf wheat variety that performs reliably on the North China Plain. Before sowing, I will plough the field to break up the soil and bury the previous maize residue, which helps with water retention over the winter. For fertilizer, I will apply a compound NPK blend as a base and then topdress urea at the wheat jointing stage in spring; my total nutrient plan is about 16 kg nitrogen, 7 kg phosphorus, and 6 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate three times using my well: once before winter to ensure good emergence and safe overwintering, once at jointing, and once during grain filling. I will spray twice—once for weeds and once to control powdery mildew or aphids if they appear, which they usually do in our humid summers.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I have a very narrow window to plant summer maize, so I will use no-tillage seeding to save time, fuel, and soil moisture. I will plant a hybrid maize variety with good density tolerance and disease resistance. I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing and side-dress urea at the big-flare stage, totaling about 17 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate twice if the summer drought sets in—at jointing/tasseling and at grain filling. Two pesticide applications will suffice: a pre-emergence or early post-emergence herbicide, and one insecticide spray to control Asian corn borer. I expect around 550 kg/mu from the wheat and 600 kg/mu from the maize, which are solid, realistic targets for well-managed land here.
